textbookBox.concept: The frog jumps 3 steps at a time and lands on 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 and 18, and these numbers are called multiples of 3.

beats.en: The frog jumps 3 steps at a time and lands on 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 and 18, and these numbers are called multiples of 3. Look at the number line on the board, where each jump of 3 starts where the last one ended.

beats.en: Some numbers are touched by two animals, and these are called common multiples. The frog and the squirrel both touch 12, 24 and 36, so these are common multiples of 3 and 4.

textbookBox.concept: If the cat and the rat land on the same number, the cat catches the rat. The cat starts on 6 and jumps 3 steps each time, while the rat starts on 12 and jumps 2 steps each time.

beats.en: Gulabo’s lily flowers each have 3 petals, so 12 flowers have 12 × 3 petals. We can break 12 into 10 and 2, so 10 × 3 is 30 petals, 2 × 3 is 6 petals and together that is 36 petals.

textbookBox.ref: CBSE Class 4 maths · Equal Groups · Complete Summary
textbookBox.concept: A hibiscus flower has 5 petals and Gulabo counted 80 petals in all, so the number of flowers is 80 ÷ 5. 10 petals make 2 flowers and 50 petals make 10 flowers, so 80 petals make 16 flowers.

beats.en: Let us review the key takeaway from Equal Groups: A hibiscus flower has 5 petals and Gulabo counted 80 petals in all, so the number of flowers is 80 ÷ 5. 10 petals make 2 flowers and 50 petals make 10 flowers, so 80 petals make 16 flowers.
